nameStory: This plant earned its common name because European explorers first encountered it as a leafy green vegetable in New Zealand, where indigenous Māori people had long harvested it. The name stuck even though we now know it's actually native to a much wider area including Australia and eastern Asia, making its way around the world's coastlines.
description: New Zealand spinach is a sprawling, succulent annual that looks quite different from regular spinach. It forms low, spreading mats with thick, fleshy triangular leaves that feel almost rubbery to the touch. The plant can spread several feet across, hugging sandy ground with its trailing stems, and produces tiny inconspicuous flowers tucked among the leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy triangular or diamond-shaped leaves that feel succulent and slightly rubbery when squeezed, with a waxy surface that helps them retain moisture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, sprawling mats that spread horizontally along the ground rather than growing upright, with trailing stems that can extend several feet

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers with no petals that are easily missed, tucked into leaf joints rather than displayed prominently

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy reddish or green stems that feel firm and succulent, often with a slightly crystalline or bumpy texture when touched

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found in sandy, salty environments near the coast where few other leafy plants can survive the harsh conditions

habitat: In New England, New Zealand spinach is most likely found along sandy coastlines, beach edges, and disturbed sandy areas near salt water. It thrives in places where salt spray reaches and regular plants struggle, often growing in pure sand or sandy soil mixed with seaweed and debris. Look for it in areas that get some disturbance from storms, foot traffic, or coastal erosion.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate as soil warms, with first succulent leaves emerging in late spring. Young plants are small and easily overlooked at this stage.
seasonality.summer: Prime growing season when the plant spreads into distinctive mats and produces its tiny flowers. Leaves are at their most succulent and identifiable during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Plants continue growing until first frost, often looking their most robust in early fall. Seeds ripen and scatter during this period.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely with frost, leaving only seeds in the sandy soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: This plant is basically nature's salt-filtering machine - it can actually grow in soil so salty that it would kill most other plants, making it one of the few leafy greens that thrives where ocean spray regularly hits the ground.
confusionNotes: The thick, triangular succulent leaves make it quite distinctive and unlikely to be confused with other plants. Regular spinach has thin, non-succulent leaves and grows upright rather than in spreading mats.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's from New Zealand, this plant is actually native to much of the Pacific Rim. It's been used as a food plant for thousands of years and was one of the first 'exotic' vegetables brought back to Europe by Captain Cook's expeditions.
compareHints: New Zealand spinach is the only member of its genus found in New England, making it unique in the region. Within its stone plant family, it's distinguished from other succulents by its large, triangular leaves and sprawling coastal habitat, while most other family members are small, compact desert plants with tiny leaves.
